assetsBodyV2:
All programming languages within the explicitly listed in-scope assets are covered, subject to this policy’s exclusions.

Client source baseline: base/base v1.6.0-rc.9, commit [689054ee14933cb2ee5bd54eadcd8dacbe1cc517](https://github.com/base/base/tree/689054ee14933cb2ee5bd54eadcd8dacbe1cc517). Its declared base/reth dependency is 2b20e42de9c42b51ea0fb56599fda3c2f22640ef. The client pin does not automatically include every dependency/component or finalize the other repositories' scope. Deployed contracts in scope, below, lists each contract's address, implementation, version and source revision.

__Networks and code in scope__

Everest will not be live on Sepolia during the competition; it is tested on the designated local Everest devnet built from the pinned commit (just devnet up everest). The Base-native contracts deployed on Base are in scope: AggregateVerifier, TEEVerifier, DisputeGameFactory, AnchorStateRegistry, TEEProverRegistry, ProtocolVersions, NitroValidator, CertManager and P384Verifier (github.com/base/nitro-validator at 0ea0d123). Contracts inherited from Optimism that Base does not deploy are out of scope even though they appear in base/contracts: SuperFaultDisputeGame and super-root game types, OPSuccinctFaultDisputeGame and its AccessManager, OPContractsManager. The legacy fault-proof contracts still deployed on Ethereum Sepolia (FaultDisputeGame, PermissionedDisputeGame, MIPS, PreimageOracle and their DelayedWETH proxies) are also out of scope.

Everest scope covers Base Transactions (EIP-8430, type 0x79) and gas-limit billing at the immutable base/base commit in Assets in Scope. This includes transaction encoding, authorization, replay protection, execution, settlement, native nonce/context precompiles, payer RPC when enabled, admission, block building, receipts, batch encoding/derivation and the proof-boot Everest gate. Use the Base-transactions/base-tx names at the recorded rc.9 pin. Historical EIP-8130 names do not exclude retained functionality.

Gas-limit billing is in scope for standard user transactions and Base Transactions when it is enabled in the Everest environment, including execution and proving consistency, settlement, builder reservations, and receipt and header accounting.

OP-derived contracts that Base deployed are in scope as listed in Deployed contracts in scope, below: OptimismPortal2, SystemConfig, DisputeGameFactory, L2ToL1MessagePasser, L1Block, the fee vaults, the bridge and messenger contracts and their factories, and the listed L2 predeploys.

The pinned code defines the implementation under review. This policy defines scope, intended security requirements and eligible impacts. Code takes precedence over the EIP and documentation for implementation details, but an implementation bug is not intended behavior merely because it exists in the code. A discrepancy without an in-scope impact is not eligible for a reward.

The in-scope deployment pipeline is base/contract-deployments. Deployment scripts inside base/contracts, such as those that wire MockVerifier, are test tooling and out of scope. Legacy endpoints that are no longer provisioned, such as the authenticated websocket-proxy endpoint, are out of scope.

__Deployed contracts in scope__

The tables below list the contracts deployed on Ethereum Sepolia (chain ID 11155111) and Base Sepolia (chain ID 84532), and the native contracts of base/base. Addresses, implementations and versions were read on 16 November 2026 at Ethereum Sepolia block 12,149,624 and Base Sepolia block 59,691,356. These deployments run earlier revisions than the pinned commit and do not include Everest. They matter only for findings that depend on deployed pre-Everest state, tested on a local fork (see PoC Requirements). Source revisions: base/contracts v8.4.0 (8c21f6d0) for the Denim, 20 October and 4 November deployments, and v8.3.0 (385f21a4) for the Cobalt deployment; base/nitro-validator 0ea0d123; deployment records in base/contract-deployments e6797dfd. Exceptions, where the deployed code is not one of these revisions: AnchorStateRegistry runs v8.0.0 (ddd5a09e) plus the patch [https://github.com/immunefi-team/audit-comp-base-everest-contract-deployments/blob/e6797dfd6ac03b35d0ddd7eb369ab94bbc5fcd31/archive/legacy/sepolia/2026-04-20-activate-multiproof/patch/asr-reset-anchor-game.patch](https://github.com/immunefi-team/audit-comp-base-everest-contract-deployments/blob/e6797dfd6ac03b35d0ddd7eb369ab94bbc5fcd31/archive/legacy/sepolia/2026-04-20-activate-multiproof/patch/asr-reset-anchor-game.patch) from the 20 April 2026 multiproof activation, and still reports 3.7.0; DelayedWETH (Multiproof) runs v8.0.0 (ddd5a09e) from the same deployment, without a patch; SystemConfig runs v8.3.0 (385f21a4) plus the patch [https://github.com/immunefi-team/audit-comp-base-everest-contract-deployments/blob/e6797dfd6ac03b35d0ddd7eb369ab94bbc5fcd31/archive/evm/2026-09-14-cobalt-upgrade/patch/max-gas-limit.patch](https://github.com/immunefi-team/audit-comp-base-everest-contract-deployments/blob/e6797dfd6ac03b35d0ddd7eb369ab94bbc5fcd31/archive/evm/2026-09-14-cobalt-upgrade/patch/max-gas-limit.patch)applied to the listed Sepolia deployment, hence its version 3.14.0+max-gas-limit-2000M. Everest uses the native precompiles of the designated local Everest devnet, built from the competition commit. At that commit, the devnet deploys its L1 contracts from the artifacts bundled with its setup tooling, not from base/contracts v8.5.0-rc.1. Base fixed this on main in base/base#6680 (base/base#6680). To use it, apply base/base#6682 and then base/base#6680 on top of the competition commit, in that order (base/base#6680 does not apply on its own); just devnet up everest then builds the L1 contracts and L2 predeploys from base/contracts v8.5.0-rc.1 (b9b76d97). Both change only the devnet setup, not in-scope code. The Everest devnet still runs no proposer, prover or challenger; proof components follow the proof-component PoC exception.

__Production configuration__

The values below describe the typical Base setup after Everest: the configuration Base runs today with Denim, which it expects to keep when Everest activates. PoCs use this configuration on the designated local Everest devnet (see Everest environment, below, and PoC Requirements). Lines marked “On Sepolia” describe the pre-Everest deployments and apply only to findings tested on a local fork. They are facts for this competition, even where the configuration files sit in folders that are otherwise out of scope, such as base/base/etc. Findings that only appear under a different configuration are out of scope unless the report shows an unprivileged way to reach it.

- Operator fee: operatorFeeScalar = operatorFeeConstant = 0.
- Resource metering is an optional optimization, off by default, and fails open by design. The local devnet turns it on for base-builder (--builder.enable-resource-metering in etc/docker/docker-compose.yml); remove that flag when preparing the competition test environment. This is a testing-configuration override, not a change to the audited implementation. Base made the same change on main in [base/base#6682](https://github.com/base/base/pull/6682), which also applies cleanly to the competition commit.
- Bundles are not live and are not a private order-flow mechanism.
- The following experimental or testing modes are excluded from the competition’s scope:
  - Shadow indexing: --enable-shadow-indexer.
  - Shadow sequencing: --sequencer.shadow-blocks-per-cycle and --sequencer.shadow-funding-*.
  - Consensus development RPC: --rpc.dev-enabled.
  - Dangerous L1 overrides: overrides of the DA batch inbox or batcher sender.
  - Deferred validity-signature mode: --validity-signature-mode.
  - Experimental Reth synchronization and networking: --snap.v2 and --net-if.experimental.
  - Research-only transaction limits: --pooled-tx-response-soft-limit and --pooled-tx-pack-soft-limit.
  - Reth development and testing modes: --dev*, --testing.* and the testing_buildBlockV1 RPC.
  - Reth debug CLI modes: --debug.*, including options that skip state-root or genesis validation, simulate reorgs or consensus, or skip fork-choice updates or new-payload processing. These CLI modes are distinct from debug builds and debug_* RPC methods.
  - Experimental engine-tuning options: --engine.txpool-prewarming, --engine.share-sparse-trie-with-payload-builder, --engine.suppress-persistence-during-build, --engine.prewarm-reuse, --engine.state-root-task-compare-updates, --engine.disable-sparse-trie-cache-pruning and --engine.disable-bal-*.
  - Payer relay on RPC nodes: --rollup.payer-enabled / --rollup.payer serve payer_getTerms and payer_sendTransaction. Off by default and not set anywhere.

These exclusions apply only to findings that require the listed unsupported modes or settings. Shared code reachable under the supported competition configuration remains in scope. Using an approved local test harness does not itself make a finding out of scope.

  - Base batcher’s enabled shadow mode (BASE_BATCHER_SHADOW_ENABLED) remains in scope. It is distinct from the excluded shadow-indexer and shadow-sequencer modes
- Block production: on the designated local Everest devnet, base-builder runs as the sequencer and, after Denim, builds each block once with the native payload builder; base-client follows it and forwards transactions to it. Batching: op-batcher v1.16.5 with Base Transaction support (base/optimism op-batcher/v1.16.5-basetx.2) posts singular batches; base-batcher runs in shadow mode with its own key and a separate shadow inbox.
- Cancun and later hardforks are active; pre-Cancun code paths are unreachable.
- AggregateVerifier 0.3.0 has a slow interval of 600/30 and a fast interval of 6000/300 (20 intermediate roots each), chosen per game from its starting block. The fast interval starts at ProtocolVersions index 13 (Denim); Denim is active, so PoCs use 6000/300.
- ZK verifier: AggregateVerifier uses ZkVerifier; on Sepolia, version 0.1.0 at 0xa738E13d97A3f10b307C2CD190edd3E227A72D68.
- TEE prover fleet: 4 instances, each with 39.06 GiB (40,000 MiB) of enclave memory. This has been Base’s typical setup since Base Azul and is expected for Everest; Base may run fewer instances at low load and scales up (as high as 16) to recover after downtime.
- On Sepolia, OptimismPortal2.proofMaturityDelaySeconds = 0 and AnchorStateRegistry.disputeGameFinalityDelaySeconds = 0: a withdrawal can be finalized in the block after its game resolves. This applies only to findings tested on a local fork of Sepolia. PoCs use the Base mainnet values: both delays are 1 day, with the dispute windows in Assumptions about Base’s response (5 days with one accepted proof; 1 day after a second proof of the other type).
- Everest environment (the designated local Everest devnet, just devnet up everest: Azul, Beryl, Cobalt and Denim activate at L2 blocks 20, 21, 22 and 25, and Everest at block 100):
  - Gas-limit billing is active: every non-deposit transaction is billed for its gas limit, plus the payer authentication cost for a sponsored Base Transaction.
  - Keystore code is removed at the competition commit: only secp256k1 sender and payer authentication remain, and delegation (type 0x01) is the only account change, at most one per transaction. Zenith is an empty, genesis-only upgrade that gates no execution behavior, and proof boot rejects it.
  - The payer RPC (payer_getTerms, payer_sendTransaction) is disabled by default.
  - Mempool ordering by declared coinbase tip divided by gas_limit; per-account limits of 16 per payer (a self-paying sender counts as its own payer) and 64 per allowlisted payer. The per-sender limit and the --rollup.mempool-sender-limit and --rollup.mempool-trusted-delegation-targets flags were removed.
  - Base cost of 12,000 gas; payer authentication is a fixed 5,100 gas (secp256k1 recovery 3,000 plus one cold read 2,100), billed on top of gas_limit for a sponsored transaction; MAX_CALL_PHASES_PER_TX = 1,024; MAX_ACCOUNT_CHANGES_PER_TX = 1.
  - Nonce-free window of 30,000 ms at inclusion and 20,000 ms in the mempool; replay ring of 340,000 entries.
  - Signature and replay domains: 0x7900 (sender), 0x7901 (payer) and 0x7902 (replay_id).
  - Execution client dependency: github.com/base/reth at 2b20e42de9c42b51ea0fb56599fda3c2f22640ef, as recorded in the deployment manifest.

__Build Commands, Test Commands, and How to Run Them__

Detailed build commands, test commands and run instructions are in the README files and documentation of each repository:

- Offchain components: [https://github.com/immunefi-team/audit-comp-base-everest-base](https://github.com/immunefi-team/audit-comp-base-everest-base)
- Deployment and upgrade scripts: [https://github.com/immunefi-team/audit-comp-base-everest-contract-deployments](https://github.com/immunefi-team/audit-comp-base-everest-contract-deployments)
- Implementation contracts: [https://github.com/immunefi-team/audit-comp-base-everest-contracts](https://github.com/immunefi-team/audit-comp-base-everest-contracts)
- TEE attestation contracts: [https://github.com/immunefi-team/audit-comp-base-everest-nitro-validator](https://github.com/immunefi-team/audit-comp-base-everest-nitro-validator)

__Asset Accuracy Assurance__

Bugs found on assets incorrectly listed in-scope are valid.

__Code Update Assurance__

Duplicate submissions of bugs are valid until the relevant bug fix is public. Once a fix is public, the bug is out of scope and later submissions of it are invalid.

A fix is public when it is listed in the Mid-Contest Changelog on this page with its UTC timestamp. Base adds every public PR or commit that fixes a security issue to the changelog within 24 hours of it becoming public, and announces it in the competition Discord channel. Reports submitted before the changelog timestamp are eligible, including as duplicates. Reports submitted after it are invalid.

A fix or advisory published after a submission does not, by itself, establish that the report is valid or set its severity.

The project commits to keeping all information about bug findings private until each fix is disclosed through the process described in the Bug Fix Policy below. This includes bug findings found independently by the project or from concurrent private audits.

Any necessary change must be documented, timestamped and communicated by Base and Immunefi. Changes must not retroactively invalidate eligible submissions or reduce accrued eligibility; define prospective treatment and any researcher-beneficial clarification explicitly.

__Code Freeze Assurance__

The commits listed in Assets in Scope are the competition baseline. The codebase is not frozen: Base may apply fixes during the competition under the Bug Fix Policy in Impact Terms.

__Mid-Contest Changelog__

Each entry lists the UTC timestamp, the PR or commit, and the issue it fixes. No entries yet.

__KYC Requirement__

Researcher KYC is required for payouts and is intended to be collected and processed by Immunefi or its disclosed KYC provider, not delivered to Coinbase. The following information will be required:

- Full name
- Date of birth
- Proof of address (either a redacted bank statement with address or a recent utility bill)
- Copy of Passport or other Government issued ID

Security researchers are required to submit KYC within 7 days of KYC being requested, else their rewards may be forfeited. Immunefi may make exceptions due to extenuating circumstances.

For the full process, see KYC Process for Audit Competitions (link: [https://immunefisupport.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/32264466580497](https://immunefisupport.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/32264466580497)).

__Standardized Rules__

This competition follows Immunefi's standard competition rules. For the full default rules on validity, duplicates, known issues, severity, disputes, KYC, payments, and publication, read How Audit Competitions Work: Rules and Policies. Where this program page defines a specific rule, the program page prevails.

__Primacy of Impact vs Primacy of Rules__

Base adheres to the Primacy of Rules, meaning the whole program is run strictly under the terms and conditions stated on this page.

__Insights__

Insight reports are not accepted in this competition. Every report must demonstrate an in-scope impact with a runnable PoC; reports that only describe best practices, code quality, documentation differences or theoretical concerns are closed.

__Duplicates and repeated reports__

Base never closes a duplicate of a valid report. It marks the report as a duplicate of the earliest one, and Immunefi applies the duplicate reward rule. A later report of the same root cause by the same researcher is closed in favour of their first report. Each report must cover one root cause; triage splits reports that mix several. All reports of one root cause receive the same classification.

__Dispute Resolution__

Disputes may only address report validity, duplicate determinations, and severity.

If a researcher disagrees with a closure decision while the competition is live, they may request mediation. A mediation fee, set by Immunefi, is required to initiate the review.

After the evaluation phase, a dispute period opens for appealing decisions. Immunefi announces a final 48-hour deadline for the last disputes. Once the window closes, results are final.

Immunefi has final say on validity, duplicates, and severity, based on the terms of this program.

Base replies to each mediation request within 5 business days.

__Responsible Publication Policy__

Immunefi will publish bug reports, earnings, and a leaderboard for this Audit Competition.

Security Researchers may publish their bug reports as well, but only after Immunefi has published the valid bug reports as part of the competition results.

**Eligibility Criteria** Security researchers who wish to participate must adhere to the rules of engagement set forth in this program and cannot be:

- On OFACs SDN list
- Official contributor, both past or present
- Employees and/or individuals closely associated with the project
- Security auditors that directly or indirectly participated in an audit review of the code in scope (Such auditors may still participate in this program only if they receive project permission)
- From a restricted country or territory per Immunefi's Terms of Use (link: [https://immunefi.com/terms-of-use/](https://immunefi.com/terms-of-use/))
- Under 18 years of age. Participants under 18 cannot pass KYC and will not receive rewards.

__Submission Fees__

A submission fee, set and managed by Immunefi, applies to each report and is shown at submission time. If a researcher disagrees with a closure decision, initiating a mediation also requires a fee set by Immunefi.

Rewards are distributed among SRs according to Immunefi’s Standardized Competition Reward Terms and include the All Star Pool and Podium Pool reserved for All Star Program participants.

Rewards are denominated in USD and distributed in USDC on Base.

The total reward pool, shared among eligible researchers under Immunefi’s distribution rules, is determined by the highest-severity valid finding.

- A Critical is found - USD 250,000
- A High is found - USD 125,000
- A Medium is found - USD 70,000
- A Low is found - USD 30,000
- If none of the above conditions apply, the reward pool is USD 20,000

Private known issues, meaning known issues that were not publicly disclosed, are valid and unlock the corresponding reward pool.

A private known issue that is publicly disclosed during the competition becomes a public known issue, as set out in the Private Known Issues Reward Policy.

Immunefi will administer researcher payouts from the prepaid reward pool. After the competition has concluded and the final bug reports have been resolved, rewards are distributed all at once based on Immunefi’s distribution formula.
impactsBody:
Impacts In Scope

Only the following impacts are accepted within this program. All other impacts are not considered as in-scope, even if they affect something in the assets in scope table. Where a report demonstrates more than one impact, the highest applicable demonstrated impact governs. An impact that is claimed but not demonstrated does not raise the severity.

__Proof of Concept (PoC) Requirements__

A runnable PoC is required for every report, whatever its severity. Reports without a runnable PoC are closed. For more information, please read the [Web3 PoC Guidelines](https://immunefisupport.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/18722863230353).

The PoC must execute the in-scope code path that contains the bug, with the Production configuration in Assets in Scope, including signature checks and gossip validation. Outside the proof-component PoC exception below, a PoC that replaces a trusted component (preimage oracle, L1 provider, state database or verifier) with a mock that breaks that component’s contract is invalid. For enclave code, the local server harness is accepted if it runs the same request-handling code.

Where the PoC runs:

- Default: the designated local Everest devnet built from the competition commit (just devnet up everest), with the Production configuration, real binaries and default flags, and resource metering disabled (see Production configuration). This applies to Beryl, Cobalt, Denim and Everest code: Denim’s 200 ms cadence is active from L2 block 25 and Everest from block 100. PoCs for block production, derivation, timing or node resources report the measured timestamp lag or resource change against a baseline run. Mocks of the executor or the transaction pool are not accepted.
- Local forks: a local fork of Ethereum Sepolia, Base Sepolia, Ethereum mainnet or Base mainnet is allowed only when the exploit requires state that exists only on that network. Forks only, never the live network. A fork does not bring that network’s deployments into scope; the PoC must still execute in-scope code. A Base Sepolia fork for Denim timing starts at block 48,418,656 or later.
- Contracts at base/contracts v8.5.0-rc.1: a Foundry test in base/contracts at the competition commit (b9b76d97) that deploys the affected contracts with the Production configuration values, or the local devnet with base/base#6682 and #6680 applied (see Deployed contracts in scope).
- Proof components: the proof-component PoC exception below.
- Validity transactions: a local devnet only. Testing against the public sequencer endpoint is prohibited.

Proof-component PoC exception:

For in-scope proof programs, prover services, proposer/challenger logic and proof-verification contracts, runnable component-level PoCs are accepted. Researchers are not required to operate the complete proposer, prover and challenger stack or reproduce Base’s production proving infrastructure. The PoC must execute the affected in-scope code at the competition’s specified revision and applicable configuration.

Test fixtures, local harnesses and mocks may supply surrounding dependencies, provided they do not fabricate the vulnerability or bypass the security property being tested. For example, a local harness that bypasses hardware attestation may support a finding unrelated to attestation, but cannot establish an attestation bypass. Reports must identify mocked or substituted dependencies, explain what the PoC demonstrates, and distinguish demonstrated effects from remaining integration assumptions.

A report will not be rejected solely because the researcher cannot run the complete proof stack or access production proving infrastructure. Where end-to-end reproduction is limited by those requirements, Base and Immunefi will assess the runnable component-level reproduction and supporting evidence, with Base assisting in integration validation where needed. Final severity depends on the validated impact; a component-level defect does not automatically establish a higher-severity end-to-end outcome. In Proof soundness and Invalid output roots, severity follows the furthest stage that the PoC demonstrates or that Base’s integration validation confirms; a confirmed stage counts as demonstrated.

This exception applies only to the listed proof components that are already in scope. It does not expand asset scope, permit live-network testing, or relax the requirements for unrelated execution, sequencing, batching or validity-transaction findings. For findings spanning execution and proofs, the relevant execution behavior must still be faithfully reproduced. All other policy requirements remain unchanged.

Researchers may amend the PoC or the selected impact until the competition end date. Triage and mediation assess the report as it stands on that date.

__Definitions__

For this L2, “network not being able to confirm new transactions” means an unprivileged exploit prevents the sequencer from including otherwise-valid, adequately funded and fee-paying user transactions available to it for at least 30 seconds. Blocks that contain only the L1-info and BaseTime deposits count as not confirming user transactions.

A network processing node is shut down when it stops processing new blocks and does not recover without a manual restart. A total network shutdown is the Critical impact defined above.

An exploit through base_sendRawTransactionValidity is rated under the impact it demonstrates: Network not being able to confirm new transactions (Critical) when it stops user-transaction inclusion for at least 30 seconds; otherwise the node-shutdown or resource-consumption impacts. Degradation caused by volume alone is out of scope.

__B20 impacts__

Severity is assessed as if the token held mainnet value. A standalone policy or pause bypass without a demonstrated Critical impact is High. B20 balances, minting, roles, policies and pauses use the B20 and Smart Contract impacts, even though their implementation includes Rust precompiles. Execution or proving divergence and network availability use the Blockchain/DLT impacts.

__Smart Contract impacts__

Applies to base/contracts (multiproof system: AggregateVerifier, TEEVerifier, DisputeGameFactory, TEEProverRegistry), base/nitro-validator (NitroValidator, CertManager, P384Verifier) and base/contract-deployments (deployment and upgrade scripts).

__Proof soundness__

“Invalid TEE or ZK proof” means a proof accepted only through key compromise, forged attestation or a cryptographic break of the prover. Reports that rely on one are out of scope unless they show how to obtain it. A bug in NitroValidator, CertManager or P384Verifier that accepts an attestation AWS did not sign is a way to obtain one and stays in scope.

A valid proof that the deployed TEE or ZK program produces for a state transition different from canonical Base execution is a proof-soundness bug. It is Critical when the invalid root can also finalize despite Base’s Security Council and Guardian emergency actions (blacklisting or retiring the game), High when the PoC reaches AggregateVerifier acceptance or stops at the verifier library, and Medium when it stops at proof generation. Assumption (b) in Assumptions about Base’s response does not apply.

Invalid output roots. A report that causes AggregateVerifier to accept an invalid output root, or a game to resolve or a withdrawal to finalize against one, is Critical, whatever the path: a forged or bypassed proof, a schedule defect or a timing defect. Assumption (b) may lower it by one level, once. A proof-soundness bug or an execution divergence is the exception: acceptance alone is High, and it is Critical only when the invalid root can also finalize despite Base’s Security Council and Guardian emergency actions. A bug that stops before AggregateVerifier accepts the root is rated by the stage it reaches, as set out above.

__Optional Project Info__

__Where might Security Researchers confuse out-of-scope code to be in-scope?__

Given Base’s previous status as an OP Stack chain, participants may confuse OP Stack components (op-node, op-geth, op-batcher) as in scope. Only Base-native code in the Assets in Scope section is in scope. Optimism contracts that Base does not deploy are out of scope. The ZK host and its circuits (the zkVM program), including the changes Base made to OP-Succinct, are in scope. Soundness bugs in the zkVM are not in scope. See Networks and code in scope.

__Is this an upgrade of an existing system? If so, which? And what are the main differences?__

Everest adds Base Transactions (EIP-8430) and gas-limit billing. The competition also covers the Beryl, Cobalt and Denim components listed in Assets in Scope. Base Azul introduced the earlier changes below:

- Client consolidation: migrating from op-geth and op-node to base-reth-node (EL) and base-consensus (CL).
- Proof system migration: replacing Optimistic fault proofs (Cannon) with a dual-proof system (TEE and ZK) for faster finality.
- Custom features: Fusaka EIP support and future protocol innovations. See [https://specs.base.org/upgrades/v1/overview](https://specs.base.org/upgrades/v1/overview) for more details.

__Where do you suspect there may be bugs and/or what attack vectors are you most concerned about?__

Primary areas for review, subject to Assets in Scope:

- Offchain consensus and execution logic: state root derivation bugs in base-consensus and base-reth-node.
- Proof system integration: TEE and ZK dispute game submission logic, verifier contract bugs, and soundness issues in ZK recursion.
- Protocol transitions: incorrect hardfork activation logic, backwards compatibility breaks, and edge cases in EIP-1559 fee calculation.
- Multi-client discrepancies: execution differences between CL and EL that cause chain forks.

__What ERC20 / ERC721 / ERC777 / ERC1155 token standards are supported?__

At the execution layer, Base can run EVM-compatible ERC20, ERC721, ERC777 and ERC1155 contracts. The canonical bridge interfaces listed in the deployment manifest cover ERC20 and ERC721, subject to their documented token requirements; this does not imply dedicated ERC777 or ERC1155 bridging support. B20 exposes its documented ERC20-compatible interface and Base-specific extensions. Compatibility does not make third-party tokens or bridges in scope. A report must demonstrate an eligible impact in an in-scope Base component under the competition configuration.

__What emergency actions may you want to use as a reason to downgrade an otherwise valid bug report?__

Base does not close reports on the basis of its own response. The assumptions Base relies on, and the one-level downgrades they allow, are listed in Assumptions about Base’s response in Impact Terms.

What addresses would you consider any bug report requiring their involvement to be out of scope, as long as they operate within the privileges attributed to them?

Every trusted role listed in the next answer, when acting within the privileges attributed to it.

What addresses would you consider any bug report requiring their involvement be out of scope, even if they exceed the privileges attributed to them?

- The trusted roles: the sequencer, batcher, proposer, TEE signers and registrar, Security Council and Guardian. See Trust boundaries in Out of Scope & Rules.
- L1 Ethereum validators and stakers, which are not relevant to Base consensus.
- Third-party bridge validators (Relay, Across, Axelar and others), which are outside Base’s control.
- Base corporate infrastructure that is not part of the protocol (KMS, deployment pipelines and similar).

__Which chains and/or networks will the code in scope be deployed to?__

- Base Sepolia testnet for Beryl, Cobalt and Denim, and the designated local Everest devnet for Everest.
- Base mainnet, Zeronet and other devnets are out of scope, except for the local environments expressly permitted in the PoC Requirements.

__What external dependencies are there?__

- Ethereum mainnet (L1): state root anchoring, EIP-4844 blob data availability and gas price feeds.
- SP1 ZK prover: SP1 v6.10.0, with SP1 cluster v2.9.0.
- AWS Nitro Enclaves: TEE attestation infrastructure.
- Optimism upstream libraries (op-batcher, optimism/contracts) for bridge and withdrawal logic. No modifications to these libraries are in scope.
- [Base's Reth fork, github.com/base/reth at 2b20e42de9c42b51ea0fb56599fda3c2f22640ef: the execution client dependency recorded in Assets in Scope.](https://github.com/base/reth/tree/2b20e42de9c42b51ea0fb56599fda3c2f22640ef)

__Are there any unusual points about your protocol that may confuse Security Researchers?__

The full list is in Intended behavior in Out of Scope & Rules. The points researchers most often misread:

- Single-proof finality model: a TEE or ZK proof is needed to finalize. A ZK proof can be used to challenge a TEE proof, but not the reverse.
- Intermediate output roots: proofs cover block ranges and commit to intermediate roots within a proposal, so disputes can cover a much smaller range of blocks.
- Soundness alert mechanism: if two different state roots both have valid proofs of the same type (both TEE or both ZK), the game can be automatically nullified.

What are the most valuable educational resources already available? (Ie. Documentation, Explainer videos or articles, etc)

- [https://specs.base.org/upgrades/v1/overview](https://specs.base.org/upgrades/v1/overview): full V1 (Base Azul) specification.
- [https://docs.base.org/base-chain/node-operators/base-v1-upgrade](https://docs.base.org/base-chain/node-operators/base-v1-upgrade): operator migration guide.
- [https://github.com/base/base](https://github.com/base/base): open-source code with README and architecture docs.
- [https://blog.base.dev](https://blog.base.dev): technical blog posts on proofs and the stack migration.

__Previous Audits__

Base’s completed audit reports are listed below. Unfixed vulnerabilities mentioned in these reports, including their accepted-risk sections, are not eligible for a reward.

- Multiproof contracts audit 1: [https://cantina.xyz/portfolio/25ba64ea-d6f3-411e-8338-419ffc385ba6](https://cantina.xyz/portfolio/25ba64ea-d6f3-411e-8338-419ffc385ba6)
- Multiproof contracts audit 2: [https://cantina.xyz/portfolio/b72c7078-f6da-4074-a3bd-4f938f469fb7](https://cantina.xyz/portfolio/b72c7078-f6da-4074-a3bd-4f938f469fb7)
- TEE contracts audit 1: [https://cantina.xyz/portfolio/423a9f33-b710-4445-a125-950b0a7771d7](https://cantina.xyz/portfolio/423a9f33-b710-4445-a125-950b0a7771d7)
- TEE contracts audit 2: [https://cantina.xyz/portfolio/a4f952cf-1c5b-4e3c-8153-c3adff899613](https://cantina.xyz/portfolio/a4f952cf-1c5b-4e3c-8153-c3adff899613)
- Denim 200 ms blocks (Cantina): [denim-200ms-blocks.pdf](https://github.com/base/base/blob/66fa9c7d1dead0fb6334b3eb1110ad66a6a63978/audits/denim/denim-200ms-blocks.pdf)
- Dynamic Upgrades contracts (Cantina): [cantina_coinbase_dynamic_upgrades_sep2026.pdf](https://github.com/base/contracts/blob/main/audits/cantina_coinbase_dynamic_upgrades_sep2026.pdf)
- Cobalt Dynamic Upgrades (Cantina): [cobalt-dynamic-upgrades.pdf](https://github.com/base/base/blob/66fa9c7d1dead0fb6334b3eb1110ad66a6a63978/audits/cobalt/cobalt-dynamic-upgrades.pdf)

- Beryl precompile storage (Cantina): [beryl-precompiles-storage.pdf](https://github.com/base/base/blob/66fa9c7d1dead0fb6334b3eb1110ad66a6a63978/audits/beryl/beryl-precompiles-storage.pdf)

- Nitro validator (Cantina, 3 August 2026): [cantina-nitro-validator-05294ec0-2026-08-03.pdf](https://github.com/base/nitro-validator/blob/main/audits/cantina-nitro-validator-05294ec0-2026-08-03.pdf)
- Audit reports for Optimism smart contracts and components, including Kona: [https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/tree/develop/docs/security-reviews#security-reviews](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/tree/develop/docs/security-reviews#security-reviews)
- Base Azul Audit Competition results: [https://immunefi.com/audit-competition/audit-comp-base-azul/](https://immunefi.com/audit-competition/audit-comp-base-azul/)

__Public Disclosure of Known Issues__

Bug reports for publicly disclosed bugs are not eligible for a reward. Known issues are:

- The issues listed in Known Issues, below.
- Unfixed findings in the audit reports listed above.
- Limitations stated in code comments or NatSpec at the in-scope tag.
- Issues publicly disclosed in the in-scope repositories before the competition starts.

Entries added after launch apply only to reports submitted after they are published.

__Known Issues__

Reports of the issues below are not eligible for a reward. Each entry covers only the behavior it describes, within its stated scope; it does not exclude other defects in the same component.

__Issues reported in public repositories__

| ID | Issue | Description and scope | Status and reference |
|---|---|---|---|

__Private Known Issues Reward Policy__

Private known issues, meaning known issues that were not publicly disclosed, are valid for a reward at their full severity and unlock the corresponding reward pool without any downgrade.

A private known issue that is publicly disclosed during the competition becomes a public known issue at the timestamp it is listed in the Mid-Contest Changelog. Reports of it submitted before that timestamp remain valid; reports submitted after it are invalid.

Public known issues are invalid.

__Bug Fix Policy__

Base may make bug fixes during the competition. Base develops these fixes in a private repository. A fix becomes public, and the bug out of scope, when Base lists it in the Mid-Contest Changelog with its UTC timestamp.

- Fixed bugs become out of scope once the fix is public, as defined in Code Update Assurance.
- Duplicate submissions of a bug are only valid if they are submitted before the fix is public.
- Once a bug fix is made public, Base provides an explanation of the bug and proof of its resolution, typically a pull request. Immunefi lists all bug fix information in the Mid-Contest Changelog and notifies researchers in the competition Discord channel.
- If a bug fix can be bypassed, the bypass is considered a new, valid, in-scope bug.
- If a code change unrelated to a bug introduces a bug, the introduced bug is considered new, valid, and in scope.
- In the rare exception where a bug fix must be made public before it can be safely disclosed, the bug is treated as a known issue and disclosure may be delayed until the fix is deployed. This prevents issue snipers from claiming other researchers' findings.

__Feasibility Limitations__

A report may be valid, cite an in-scope asset, and demonstrate an in-scope impact, while still facing real-world obstacles to executing the attack. Feasibility limitations define what may and may not be cited when evaluating those obstacles.

Assess demonstrated impact first. Feasibility affects payout, except where this policy expressly permits a severity adjustment. Any adjustment requires evidence that its stated conditions are met.

The following standards apply to this competition. Where this program page defines a specific rule, the program page prevails.

**Attack Investment Amount** A high capital requirement is generally not a valid reason to downgrade a report. Attacks requiring USD 100 million or more to execute are considered case by case. Flashloan-based attacks are valid where sufficient liquidity exists at submission or is expected within 12 months. [https://immunefisupport.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/17243068885265](https://immunefisupport.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/17243068885265)

**Attacks With A Financial Risk To The Attacker** Financial risk to the attacker only justifies a downgrade where the risk massively outweighs the reward. Low return on investment alone is not sufficient, and high risk alongside high return is not sufficient either. Evaluation is made from the perspective of an external user, not from information only the project holds. [https://immunefisupport.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/17454897136401](https://immunefisupport.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/17454897136401)

**When Is An Impactful Attack Downgraded To Griefing?** Applies to High or Critical findings where the attacker gains no profit. The baseline is that spending USD 1 to cause USD 10 or less in damage is Griefing, while spending USD 1 to cause USD 100 or more in damage is not. Ratios between these are evaluated case by case. [https://immunefisupport.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/17455102268305](https://immunefisupport.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/17455102268305)

**Chain Rollbacks** The ability to roll the chain back to a previous state is not a valid reason to downgrade impact, severity, or payout. Projects intending to rely on rollbacks as a safety mechanism should reflect that in their reward amounts rather than citing it after a report is submitted. [https://immunefisupport.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/16913153448721](https://immunefisupport.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/16913153448721)

**Pre-Impact Bug Monitoring** Where a project can objectively prove that automated tooling would prevent an exploit with 100 percent certainty, this may justify a downgrade of one severity level. Where prevention depends on human action following automated detection, the project must demonstrate 100 percent objective certainty of both detection and prevention. [https://immunefisupport.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/19430444320401](https://immunefisupport.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/19430444320401)

**Attacks Involving Access to Privileged Addresses for Smart Contract Impacts** A report is out of scope where the attack vector itself requires the use of a privileged address. It is not out of scope merely because a privileged address is affected by the exploit. Exceptions apply where a code vulnerability grants privileges the address did not originally hold, which may result in a one-level downgrade, and where an in-scope impact arises from a logic error that a privileged address can trigger, which remains valid. In those cases the impact is treated as real, but any scaling element of the reward, such as funds at risk or freezing duration, is scaled to the minimum. For the full set of standards, see Feasibility Limitation Standards: [https://immunefisupport.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/16913132495377](https://immunefisupport.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/16913132495377)

__Assumptions about Base’s response__

No assumption below closes a report on its own. Each downgrade lowers severity by exactly one level.

- (a) Out of scope: impacts that require a proposal with an invalid root to resolve without being challenged, blacklisted or retired during its full dispute window (5 days with one accepted proof; 1 day after acceptance of a second proof of the other type; as re-extended by challenge() or nullify()), unless the reported bug is itself what gets that root past proof verification or the dispute window.
- (b) Base runs base-challenger, which recomputes every proposed output root and alerts on any divergence, and the Guardian can blacklist or retire a game within its dispute window. Under Immunefi's Pre-Impact Bug Monitoring standard (see Feasibility Limitations), Base may lower the severity of a report that gets an invalid root past proof verification by exactly one level, only when Base objectively demonstrates, for that report, 100 percent certainty of both detection by base-challenger and prevention by blacklisting or retiring the game within the window.
- (c) A restart lowers severity by exactly one level only when restarting with the documented configuration clears the condition. Defects in the default or production configuration that come back after a restart, and attacks that can be repeated, are not downgraded.
- (d) Attacks that require compromising Base-operated infrastructure are out of scope under Trust boundaries in Out of Scope & Rules. This is an exclusion, not a downgrade.

customOutOfScopeInformation:
__Base-specific:__

- Findings demonstrated only on Base mainnet, the public Base Sepolia network, Zeronet or other devnets. The exceptions are the designated local Everest devnet, local forks and component-level PoCs, as permitted in the PoC Requirements.
- Contracts inherited from Optimism that Base does not deploy, and deployment scripts inside base/contracts.
- Findings that only appear under a configuration different from the Production configuration in Assets in Scope, unless the report shows an unprivileged way to reach it.
- Impacts that require a proposal with an invalid root to resolve without being challenged, blacklisted or retired during its full dispute window, as set out in Assumptions about Base’s response.
- Theoretical impacts without any proof or demonstration.
- EIP-8130 Keystore code (Zenith account configuration, non-secp256k1 authenticators, account-change types 0x02 and 0x03), removed from the recorded rc.9 baseline, and any other code gated to Zenith, unless shown reachable with only Everest active.
- crates/common/evm2, which is not the executor for Everest.
- The Base-operated token-gas payer service, which is deferred from the Everest launch. Core payer authorization and settlement, support for third-party ERC-8168 payers, and the node’s payer-rpc proxy when enabled as documented are in scope.
- Flashblocks components (builder mode, RPC methods, the websocket-proxy and flashblock_index predicates), when unused in the approved competition configuration. Shared code remains in scope when reachable in that configuration.
- The legacy NitroEnclaveVerifier, and the RISC Zero and Boundless attestation path.

__Trust boundaries:__

- Trusted roles: the sequencer, batcher, proposer, TEE signers and registrar, Security Council and Guardian. Attacks that require any of them to act maliciously or be compromised are out of scope.
- Trusted inputs: unsafe-block gossip signed by the unsafe-block signer, the Engine API, and L1/L2 RPC endpoints configured by the operator. Attacks that require malicious content from these sources are out of scope, unless the attacker can inject that content without controlling the source.
- Base-operated infrastructure: attacks that require compromising it are out of scope.
- Non-public endpoints: the admin, debug, engine, miner and txpool namespaces of base-consensus and base-reth-node, builder-internal methods such as base_insertValidatedTransaction, the prover service and the websocket-proxy origin. Public traffic reaches nodes only through proxyd method allowlisting. A missing authentication or flag check on a non-public endpoint is out of scope, unless the report shows the endpoint is reachable from an untrusted network in Base’s documented deployment. Public RPC allowlist (Base mainnet and Base Sepolia): eth_chainId, eth_blockNumber, eth_gasPrice, eth_maxPriorityFeePerGas, eth_feeHistory, eth_getBlockByHash, eth_getBlockByNumber, eth_getBlockReceipts, eth_getBlockTransactionCountByHash, eth_getBlockTransactionCountByNumber, eth_getBalance, eth_getStorageAt, eth_getTransactionCount, eth_getCode, eth_getProof, eth_call, eth_estimateGas, eth_createAccessList, eth_simulateV1, eth_getTransactionByHash, eth_getTransactionByBlockHashAndIndex, eth_getTransactionByBlockNumberAndIndex, eth_getTransactionReceipt, eth_getLogs, eth_newFilter, eth_newBlockFilter, eth_uninstallFilter, eth_getFilterChanges, eth_getFilterLogs, net_version, web3_clientVersion, eth_sendRawTransaction, eth_sendRawTransactionSync, base_sendRawTransactionValidity and base_transactionStatus. The local devnet exposes every method for testing. Local availability of an RPC method does not establish that an attacker can reach it in the supported deployment. A finding requiring a non-public method must demonstrate an unprivileged path to that method or the affected behavior. Using privileged local RPCs solely to prepare a test does not itself invalidate the PoC, provided the exploit does not depend on privileges unavailable to the attacker.
- RPC resource consumption that matches the behaviour of upstream Reth at the version Base’s fork tracks (base/reth 2b20e42d), for example eth_getLogs or debug_* methods, is out of scope. RPC code specific to Base, such as the BaseTime fields, is in scope.
- Attacks that rely on heavy volumetric flooding of the public RPC ingress nodes are out of scope, unless they cause a lasting effect that needs manual recovery, such as a chain halt. Temporary unavailability caused by a denial of service is out of scope.
- Only eth_sendRawTransaction, base_sendRawTransactionValidity, eth_sendRawTransactionSync and base_transactionStatus reach the nodes that build blocks. Other, read-only RPC methods are served by a separate set of nodes, so an issue limited to the read path cannot affect block building or the sequencer and is not rated Critical.

__Intended behavior (not vulnerabilities):__

- The L1 head (l1OriginHash) only attests that blob data came from a real L1 block. Which recent L1 block is used does not matter; the proof binds the L2 block number and state root.
- Nullifying a prover is a global kill-switch. It blocks all games and needs a Security Council upgrade to restore. Bonds stay recoverable through DelayedWETH.
- Challenges exist only to counter incorrect TEE proofs. A faulty ZK verifier is handled by nullifying it, which can be done through any unchallenged game.
- challenge() and nullify() have no gameOver() check, so invalid roots can be disputed for as long as possible.
- Child games of an invalid parent are invalid. Bonds are refunded when a game is blacklisted or retired, and are awarded only in the earliest parent game. Blacklisting stops a game from becoming the anchor; it does not claw back bonds.
- Additional proofs can only shorten a game’s resolution time.
- After retirement, recovery resets the AnchorStateRegistry anchor and deploys a new AggregateVerifier, as in contract-deployments/archive/legacy/sepolia/2026-04-20-activate-multiproof.
- TEE proofs are centralized: only Coinbase generates and submits them. The registrar treats signer discovery as the source of truth, so deregisterSigner is not a permanent revocation. The proposer discards and retries while it waits for a valid TEE signer.
- The sequencer and op-conductor cluster favours consistency: when the conductor cannot commit, block production stalls by design.
- Behaviour that follows the OP Stack specification and matches upstream op-node is not a Base-specific vulnerability.
- Gas-limit billing: a receipt’s gasUsed is the billed gas (the gas limit, plus the payer authentication cost for a sponsored Base Transaction), and the header’s gasUsed is the sum of the receipts. Unused gas and EIP-3529, EIP-7702 and precompile refunds do not reduce the fee.
- Documented exceptions: deposits keep metered gas and pay no L2 execution fee. eth_call, eth_estimateGas, eth_simulateV1 with validation=false, debug_traceCall and trace_call run without fee charging and report metered gas. Estimates for Base Transactions exclude the payer authentication cost, which settlement adds once. eth_simulateV1 rejects Base Transactions.
- The transaction hash is keccak256 of the full EIP-2718 encoding, including sender and payer authentication, so fee bumps and re-signed authentication change it. Nonce-free deduplication uses replay_id, not the transaction hash.
- A transaction that carries a delegation must use the protocol nonce (nonce key 0); a delegation on any other nonce key is rejected at inclusion. Delegation needs no separate EIP-7702 authorization, and Base never delegates automatically.
- Validity predicates are not allowed on EIP-7702 transactions, on senders delegated through EIP-7702, or on Base Transactions that carry a delegation; the transaction pool rejects them at admission.
